content: 1. Abdel Razek S. conducted clinical, biochemical, and experimental studies on lactation, specifically examining the clinical effects of steroids on the initiation of lactation. This research was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1970. 2. Massai MR and colleagues evaluated the contraceptive efficacy and clinical performance of Nestorone implants in postpartum women. Their findings were published in Contraception in 2001. 3. McCann MF and collaborators studied the effects of a 0.03 mg progestin-only contraceptive on breastfeeding. This research was published in Contraception in 1989. 4. Moggia AV and colleagues compared the use of a progestin-only oral contraceptive with non-hormonal methods in lactating women in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Their findings were published in Contraception in 1991. 5. Reinprayoon D and colleagues investigated the effects of the etonogestrel-releasing contraceptive implant (Implanon) on breastfeeding parameters compared to an intrauterine device (IUD). This study was published in Contraception in 2000. 6. Schiappacasse V and colleagues conducted a six-year follow-up study on the health and growth of infants breastfed by Norplant contraceptive implant users. Their findings were published in Contraception in 2002. 7. Seth U and colleagues examined the effects of a subdermal silastic implant containing norethindrone acetate on human lactation. This research was published in Contraception in 1977. 8. Shaaban MM reviewed the use of progestogens and progesterone for contraception during lactation. This study was published in the Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology in 1991. 9. Shaaban MM, Salem HT, and Abdullah KA studied the influence of early postpartum initiation of levonorgestrel contraceptive implants (Norplant) on lactation and infant growth. Their findings were published in Contraception in 1985. 10. Shaamash AH and colleagues conducted a comparative study of the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (Mirena) versus the Copper T380A IUD during lactation, focusing on breastfeeding performance, infant growth, and development. This research was published in Contraception in 2005. 11. Shikary ZK and colleagues investigated the pharmacodynamic effects of levonorgestrel (LNG) administered orally or subdermally to early postpartum lactating mothers, focusing on urinary levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and testosterone in their breastfed male infants. This study was published in Contraception in 1986. 12. Recommendations for the use of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) in women with specific medical conditions or characteristics were established based on the World Health Organization’s eligibility criteria for contraceptive use. These recommendations include: Young women (menarche to <18 years) can generally use DMPA (MEC Category 2). Women aged 18–45 years can use DMPA without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women >45 years can generally use DMPA (MEC Category 2). Women with endometriosis can use DMPA without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women living with HIV, regardless of disease severity, can use DMPA without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women with a BMI ≥30 kg/m² can use DMPA without restriction (MEC Category 1). 13. Evidence suggests that DMPA-SC (subcutaneous) and DMPA-IM (intramuscular) have similar safety profiles, contraceptive efficacy, and effects on weight change, bleeding patterns, and bone mineral density (BMD). However, DMPA does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV, and consistent condom use is recommended for STI prevention. 14. The Sino-implant (II), a levonorgestrel-releasing contraceptive implant, has a safety profile comparable to other LNG implants, with no significant differences in serious adverse events such as ectopic pregnancy or discontinuation due to medical problems. Studies suggest that the implant is not harmful and may be beneficial for women with menorrhagia. 15. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), including levonorgestrel (LNG), ulipristal acetate (UPA), and combined oral contraceptives (COCs), are generally safe for use in women with specific medical conditions. However, breastfeeding women are advised to avoid breastfeeding for one week after taking UPA due to its excretion in breast milk. 16. Women’s contraceptive choices are influenced by individual circumstances, societal and cultural contexts, and perceptions. 17. Studies on DMPA-SC and DMPA-IM indicate no significant differences in contraceptive efficacy, weight changes, or bleeding patterns. Both formulations are therapeutically equivalent and demonstrate high contraceptive efficacy. 18. The implant is considered safe for use in women with medical conditions. 19. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) are not indicated for pregnant women but pose no known harm if accidentally used during pregnancy. Breastfeeding women can use LNG or COCs without restriction, while UPA is generally safe but requires temporary cessation of breastfeeding. 20. The evidence supports the safety and efficacy of hormonal contraceptives, including implants and injectables, for women with various medical conditions, with recommendations tailored to individual health profiles and reproductive needs.
